written.myAnswer: A scalar quantity has magnitude only; a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
Scalars: distance, speed, time, mass, temperature. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight.
Place the tail of each vector at the head of the preceding vector. The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last.
A distance–time graph plots distance against time; a speed–time graph plots speed against time.

(i) No; constant velocity means zero acceleration. (ii) Yes; if direction changes, as in circular motion, velocity changes despite constant speed.
Distance equals the magnitude of displacement when the object moves in a straight line without reversing direction. Otherwise, displacement magnitude is less than distance.
The shorter-barrel gun has the larger acceleration, assuming both bullets start from rest: it produces the greater muzzle speed over the shorter distance, and a = v²/(2s).
Yes. The object can have negative instantaneous velocity during part of the trip while its net displacement, and hence average velocity, is positive.
The velocity–time graph is a straight line from +v at t = 0 to −v at t = T, crossing zero at T/2, because acceleration due to gravity is constant downward.

Yes. At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball’s path, its instantaneous velocity is zero while its acceleration remains g downward.
A vector is represented by a directed line segment: its length represents magnitude and its arrowhead indicates direction.
Rest: position does not change with time relative to a reference point. Motion: position changes with time relative to a reference point.
Speed is distance travelled per unit time and is scalar; velocity is displacement per unit time and is vector.
Translatory motion: motion from one place to another; rotatory motion: rotation about an axis; vibratory motion: repeated to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
Distance is the total path length and is scalar. Displacement is the change in position in a specified direction and is vector.

For constant speed, the area under a speed–time graph is a rectangle with area speed × time, which equals distance. For changing speed, the total area under the graph sums the distances covered during each time interval.
